Chromy's procedure, step by step

Source: vignettes/method.Rmd
method.Rmd

This vignette opens the machine. Nothing here is needed to use the package; it is for the reader who wants to know what is being computed, and why the answers carry an accounting of floating-point adjustments.

Expected hits and the running remainder

Write λi\lambda_i for the expected number of selections (hits) of unit ii, in list order, with ∑iλi=n\sum_i \lambda_i = n, the sample size. Split each λi\lambda_i into its integer part kik_i and fractional part rir_i. The integer parts are guaranteed: unit ii will be selected at least kik_i times. The procedure’s whole business is the fractional parts.

Walk the list accumulating the fractional parts: Fi=Fi−1+riF_i = F_{i-1} + r_i, wrapping to Fi−1F_i - 1 whenever the sum crosses one. Each crossing releases one further selection, to be given either to the unit where the crossing happened or to a unit after it. Because every ri<1r_i < 1, no unit can receive more than one of these released selections — which is why each unit’s hits are kik_i or ki+1k_i + 1 and never further from λi\lambda_i: probability minimum replacement.

The transition probabilities

What makes the procedure correct, and not merely clever, is the conditional draw at each unit. Let Ti−1T_{i-1} be the selections made so far and Ii−1I_{i-1} the selections available so far (the accumulated integer parts plus crossings). At unit ii there is at most one selection pending — Ti−1T_{i-1} is either Ii−1I_{i-1} or Ii−1−1I_{i-1} - 1 — and Chromy gives the probability that unit ii settles it, conditional on the state:

state at i−1i-1 crossing at ii probability unit ii’s extra hit occurs
nothing pending no ri/(1−Fi−1)r_i / (1 - F_{i-1})
nothing pending yes 00
one pending no 11
one pending yes Fi/Fi−1F_i / F_{i-1}

One uniform per unit decides it. These conditionals are built so that, unconditionally, each unit’s extra hit has probability exactly rir_i — the procedure is a sequential implementation of the design, not an approximation to it. Chauvet and Le Gleut (2021) give the formal properties, including the joint inclusion probabilities.

You can watch the state machine directly: the engine reports the hits and the accounting of the walk.

library(chromy)
frame <- data.frame(size = c(2.0, 0.6, 1.4, 0.3, 0.7))
s <- chromy_sample(frame, n = 5, size = "size",
                   min_replacement = TRUE, seed = 1)
s$sample[c("unit", "expected_hits", "fixed_hits", "random_hits", "hits")]
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>    unit expected_hits fixed_hits random_hits  hits
#>   <int>         <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1           2            2           0     2
#> 2     2           0.6          0           1     1
#> 3     3           1.4          1           0     1
#> 4     4           0.3          0           1     1

Unit 1, expected 2 times, carries its fixed hits; the fractional parts are settled one crossing at a time.

The head of the list

Run from a fixed first unit, the procedure would treat the units near the head subtly differently from the units near the tail. Chromy’s remedy, kept by SAS and by this package, is to draw the head itself with probability proportional to size and rotate the list to start there. With head = "residual", only units with a fractional expected hit may be drawn as the head, and the integer hits are taken as fixed.

The floating-point accounting

The arithmetic above is exact over the reals and approximate over doubles, and a sampling procedure cannot shrug at the difference: a remainder that lands at 1−10−161 - 10^{-16} either is or is not a crossing, and the answer changes who can be selected. The engine does three things about it, and reports all three rather than hiding them:

  1. The drift is measured. The expected hits are summed with compensated (Kahan) arithmetic; the difference between the sum and the integer nn must be below 10−810^{-8}, or the selection is refused — silently rescaling the caller’s probabilities would detach the weights from the design.
  2. The drift is assigned. One unit — the largest fractional part that can absorb it — takes the whole correction, so every other unit’s probability is exactly what the caller asked.
  3. Near-boundary crossings are settled. A remainder within four units in the last place of 1 is treated as a crossing, the missing sliver borrowed from the units that follow.

The accounting element of the sample says what was done; the expected_hits on the sample are always the effective ones — the denominators the estimator must use.

set.seed(42)
big <- data.frame(size = rlnorm(1000, 2))
s <- chromy_sample(big, n = 100, size = "size")
s$accounting
#> $eps_sum
#> [1] 2.590029e-14
#> 
#> $corrected_unit
#> [1] 313
#> 
#> $adjusted_crossings
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $max_adjustment
#> [1] 2.58682e-14

The estimator

With hits tit_i and effective expected hits λi\lambda_i, the multiplicity (Hansen–Hurwitz form) estimator of a total is Ŷ=∑i∈stiyi/λi\hat{Y} = \sum_{i \in s} t_i\, y_i / \lambda_i. It is design-unbiased under minimum replacement, and reduces to Horvitz–Thompson when no unit can be selected twice. For its precision no unbiased variance exists under a systematic-like design; estimate_total() uses the successive-difference estimator over the randomly decided hits, read in list order, where the serpentine sort has left genuinely similar neighbours.

References

Chromy, J. R. (1979). Sequential sample selection methods. Proceedings of the American Statistical Association, Survey Research Methods Section, 401–406.

Chauvet, G. and Le Gleut, R. (2021). Properties of Chromy’s sampling procedure. Survey Methodology, 47(2), 321–347.
